The infection process

The basic concept in the infection process is the force of infection or infectious pressure. It is commonly denoted by \(\lambda\) and is in our context space and time dependent, in which case we write \(\lambda(x,y,t)\). The interpretation of the force of infection is the rate of new cases at time \(t\) at location \((x,y)\). When considering larger areas, or time periods we can average \(\lambda(x,y,t)\) and obtain e.g. a rate per square kilometer per day, or a rate per municipality per hour. We can think also of a compartmental model, with compartments \(S\) (number of people susceptible) and \(I\) (number of people infected). The rate \(\lambda\) is then the rate with which individuals make the \(S\rightarrow I\) transition. A common choice is exponential waiting time in the \(S\) compartment. This means that the waiting time for an individual to become infected is exponentially distributed with parameter \(\lambda\). Note that this parameter can still vary across space and time, and even be dependent on \(I\) in case of communicable disease. Also, this implies that in an area with \(N\) individuals, over some time period \(T\) the number of new cases is distributed as \(\text{Poisson}(\lambda \times T \times N)\). Samples from a Poisson distribution are positive integers as required. Note that the magnitude of \(\lambda\) depends on our spatial and temporal units. A property of the Poisson distribution is that the probability of one event (per person, \(N=1\)) is \[ P_{\text{inf}} = 1-\text{e}^{-\lambda T} \tag{1}\] This may be useful in settings where individuals and events are simulated. Each time step a Bernoulli draw could be made per individual, \[ \mathcal{I} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(P_\text{inf})) \] with outcomes \(\mathcal{I}=0\) or \(\mathcal{I}=1\) according to infection occuring or not.

External force of infection

Suppose the force of infection \(\lambda=\lambda(x,y,t)\), is external, i.e. not depending on the infected individuals in the population. Then, the infection process (in case of exponentially distributed waiting times in \(S\) which we will assume from here on), can we write the average number of infected individuals in terms of a differential equation. We also assume that we are on a time scale where birth, death, and population immigration and emigration 1 can be neglected. \[ \begin{align} S'(t) &= -\lambda(t) S(t), & I'(t) &= \lambda(t) S(t),\\ S(0) &= N,&I(0) &= 0. \end{align} \] The total population is \(N\), independent of \(t\), expressed by \(S(t)+I(t)=N\). The equations are easily solved for \(I\) by first rewriting the equation for \(I\), \[ I'(t) = \lambda(t) (N-I(t)) \] We first need a general solution to the homogeneous equation, \[ \begin{aligned} I'(t) &= - \lambda(t) I(t) \Rightarrow \\ \frac{I'(t)}{I(t)} &= -\lambda(t) \Rightarrow \\ \frac{d}{dt} \ln(I(t)) &= -\lambda(t) \Rightarrow \\ \ln(I(t)) &= C_1-\int\lambda(\tau)) \, d\tau \Rightarrow \\ I(t) &= C_2 \text{e}^{-\bar{\lambda_t} t} \end{aligned} \] In the last line we defined \(\bar{\lambda_t}\) as the average \(\lambda(t)\) between zero and \(t\). Next we need a particular solution of the inhomogeneous equation: \[ I'(t) = \lambda(t) (N-I(t)) \rightarrow I(t) = N \] Finally, we add them together, and enforce boundary conditions \[ I(0) = N + C_2 \text{e}^{-\bar{\lambda_t} \times 0} =0 \Rightarrow C=-N\rightarrow I(t)=(1-e^{-\bar{\lambda_t} t}) N \tag{2}\] We observe that it is only the average infectious pressure that is relevant. Note that this equation makes perfect sense considering (Equation 1). The average number of infected at time \(t\) equals the probability of infection times the total number of individuals. The time-independent kernel falls in the framework of this section.

Link with UTwente model

The force of infection from a airborne pathgen falls under the framework of this section. Given the parameters of the kernel, we can calculate forces of infection per day per grid-cell.

Communicable disease

In case of human-to-human transmission, the force of infection is dependent on the number of individuals infected, and a factor (usually named \(\beta\)) that represents the average number of contacts per person per time unit2. Then, the differential equation becomes \[ \begin{aligned} I'(t) &= \lambda S(t) \\ &= \beta I(t) S(t) \\ &= \beta I(t) (N-I(t)) \end{aligned} \] Divide by \(I(t)(N-I(t))\), and use partial fractions to split the quotient, then recognize derivatives of a logarithm. Finally integrate the equation \[ \begin{aligned} \frac{1}{I(t)(N-I(t))}I'(t) &= \beta \Rightarrow \\ [\frac{1}{I(t)} +\frac{1}{N-I(t)}]I'(t) &= N \beta \Rightarrow \\ \frac{d}{dt}\big[ \ln(|I(t)|) + \ln(|N-I(t)|)\big] &= N \beta \Rightarrow \\ \ln(|I(t)|) - \ln(|N-I(t)| &= C_1 + \beta N t\Rightarrow \\ \frac{I(t)}{N-I(t)} &= C_2\text{e}^{\beta Nt} \Rightarrow \\ I(t) &= \frac{1}{1+C_3\text{e}^{-\beta Nt}}N \Rightarrow \\ \end{aligned} \] Now apply the initial condition \(I(0)=I_0\), \[ I_0 = \frac{N}{1+C_3} \Rightarrow C_3=(N-I_0)/I_0 \] Finally, we conclude that \(I(t)\) is a logistic function \[ I(t)=\frac{I_0 N}{I_0+(N-I_0)\text{e}^{-\beta Nt}} \tag{3}\] The fact that this function behaves completely different than (Equation 2) that will enable us to detect human-to-human transmission in the case studies.

Implementation note

Importantly, we do not use this equation, as it describes the average number of people infected. We direcly simulate the data generating process stochatsically. UTwente has an ABM model that explicitly simulates individuals and their probabilities of meeting and infecting each other.

Spillover events

The infection process within a farm as also an instance of communicable disease, and as such can also be described by a logistic equation like (Equation 3), but with different parameters. Suppose that there are \(M\) animals, with contact parameter \(\delta\), and initially one animal is infected. The force of infection to humans is proportional to the number of infected animals. Let \(\gamma\) be the parameter that combines the probability of human-animal contact and probability of human infection after contact. Then, at day \(t\), the force of infection exterted is \[ \lambda(t) = \frac{\gamma M}{1+(M-1)\text{e}^{-\delta Mt}} \] With a population at risk of \(F\) persons (e.g. farm workers, visitors), the probability of \(f\) persons infected follows a Poisson distribution with rate \(\lambda(t) F\). Whenever one or more persons got infected, spillover had occurred.

Link with WUR model

Implementation in the ADM depends on how WUR delivers the output. If it is number of infected animals per day, then it can be multiplied with the animal-human contact rate (dependent on farm managment), and probability of infection per human-animal contact (dependent on the disease) to obtain a force of infection.

The case control method

Diggle approach

Following the Diggle book, page 179, let \(\lambda(x)\) be the population intensity at location \(x\), and \(r(x)\) the probability that a person at location \(x\) is a case. Set \(c\) to be the fraction of the non-case population that is sampled as a control. Then the intensities of cases and controls are

\[\begin{aligned} \lambda_1(x) &= r(x) \lambda(x),\\ \lambda_2(x) &= c(1-r(x)) \lambda(x). \end{aligned}\]

Note that is not a matched case-control design, as the actual number of cases sampled is random. We can now calculate the probability of a person \(i\) being a case or control as

\[\begin{aligned} P(Y_i=1) &= \lambda_1(x_i)/(\lambda_1(x_i)+\lambda_2(x_i))\\ P(Y_i=0) &= \lambda_2(x_i)/(\lambda_1(x_i)+\lambda_2(x_i)). \end{aligned}\]

Set \(p_i = P(Y_i=1)\) then, we can divide the previous two equations and obtain

\[\begin{aligned} \frac{p_i}{1-p_i} & = \frac{\lambda_1(x_i)}{\lambda_2(x_i)} \\ & = c^{-1}\frac{r(x_i)}{1-r(x_i)} \rightarrow \\ \text{logit}(p_i) & = -\log(c) + \text{logit}(r(x)) \end{aligned}\]

In our case \(r(x)\) comes from a force of infection \(\psi(x)\), \[ r(x)=1-\exp(-\psi(x)) \] and

\[\begin{aligned} \text{logit}(p_i) & = -\log(c) + \log(\frac{r(x)}{1-r(x)})\\ &= -\log(c) + \log(\frac{1-\exp(-\psi(x))}{\exp(-\psi(x))})\\ &= -\log(c) + \log(\exp(\psi(x)-1)) \end{aligned}\]

Next, the force of infection comes from a kernel at unknown location \(z\), given by \[ \psi(r) = \frac{h_0}{1+(r/r_0)^\alpha } \] The force of infection experienced by person \(i\) is found by substituting the distance of the source at \(z\) to \(x_i\), \[ \psi(x_i) = \frac{h_0}{1+(\frac{||x_i-z||}{r_0})^\alpha } \] Substituting in the expression for the logit of \(p_i\):

\[\begin{aligned} \text{logit}(p_i) &= -\log(c) + \log(\exp(\frac{h_0}{1+(\frac{||x_i-z||}{r_0})^\alpha })-1) \end{aligned}\]

Note that in stan there exists the function log1m_exp to model model the last term, and also bernoulli_logit for the Bernoulli distribution on the logit scale.

Alternative approach

The approach by diggle seems attractive, since the population density drops out of the equations, and we get an expression in terms of the logit of \(p_i\). However, inspecting the log-likelihood function of the Bernoulli distribution we see \[ L = \log( p^k (1-p)^{1-k}) ) = \text{logit}(p) +\log(1-p) \] and this is still not completely written in terms of the logit of \(p\). Also the idea of sampling a fraction \(c\) of the uninfected seems strange. In reality we sample a certain number of uninfected, not dependent on the total population, but dependent on the number of cases.

Let us try to simply write down the likelihood of observing \(J\) cases and \(Q\) controls \[\begin{aligned} L &= \prod_{j=1}^J P(\text{person $j$ lives in the pixel corresponding to $x_j$})r(x_j)\\ & \prod_{q=1}^Q P(\text{person $j$ lives in the pixel corresponding to $x_j$})(1-r(x_q)) \end{aligned}\] All probabilities of living in a certain pixel are constant, and can be ignored in the likelihood. For the log-likelihood we then find \[\begin{aligned} \log(L) &= \sum_{j=1}^J \log(r(x_j)) + \sum_{q=1}^Q \log(1-r(x_q)) \\ &= \sum_{j=1}^J \log(1-\exp(-\psi(x_j))) - \sum_{q=1}^Q \psi(x_q) \end{aligned}\]

This certainly looks a lot simpler than the diggle approach, and such a likelihood can be directly code in stan using the target+= statement for incrementing the log-likelihood.

Simulation

This chapter initializes the functions needed for simulating an outbreak and creates a simulated outbreak. We first set up the study area, add inhabitants and two kernels to it. Note that distances matrices and angle-matrices are automatically pre-computed. We also demonstrate the print and plot methods.

# Define the study area
study_area_test <- studyArea$new(
  the_crs = "epsg:28992",
  res = 100,
  municipality = "De Bilt",
  study_start_date = as_date("2023-01-01"),
  study_end_date = as_date("2023-02-01")
)

k <- kernel$new(name = "test",
                x = 141470,
                y = 458960,
                r0 = 1000,
                alpha = 3.0,
                h0 = 0.1)

k2 <- anisotropic_kernel$new(name = "test aniso",
                             x = 139000,
                             y = 464000,
                             r0 = 2000,
                             alpha = 1.5,
                             h0 = 3.0,
                             mu = 0.5,
                             kappa = 2.2)

study_area_test$add_inhabitants(100)
Warning: [readValues] raster has no values
study_area_test$add_kernel(k)
study_area_test$add_kernel(k2)
study_area_test$plot()

Two ways of defining a studyArea

Study areas can also be defined in 2 different ways. Instead indicating the amount of rows and columns you can use the “res” argument to give the resolution.

study_area_test <- studyArea$new(res = 3000,
                                 study_start_date = as_date("2023-01-01"),
                                 study_end_date = as_date("2023-02-01"))
study_area_test$add_inhabitants()
Warning: [readValues] raster has no values
study_area_test$plot()

Another option is to define one or more municipalities to use as the study area.

study_area_test <- studyArea$new(municipality = c("Arnhem", "Nijmegen"),
                                 study_start_date = as_date("2023-01-01"),
                                 study_end_date = as_date("2023-02-01"))
study_area_test$add_inhabitants()
Warning: [readValues] raster has no values
study_area_test$plot()

A third option is in case you have real cases, the area is automatically defined from the true cases

# Read the real cases
outbreaks_filename <- here("data", "input",                                                 "TestDataLegionellaClusters_20231017_RDcoords.RDS")

outbreak_df <- readRDS(outbreaks_filename) %>%
  filter(str_detect(RIVMLEGICLUSTER,"Houten"))

study_dates <- outbreak_df %>%
    mutate(DateOfOnset = as_date(DateOfOnset)) %>%
    select(DateOfOnset) %>%
    transmute(start = min(DateOfOnset), end = max(DateOfOnset)) %>%
    unique()

# Initialize a study area, expecting real cases later
study_area_test <- studyArea$new(
  study_start_date = study_dates$start,
  study_end_date = study_dates$end
) # You don't define a municipality. It will be first taken the default municipality and then updated to the cases
study_area_test$add_kernel(k)  #TO BE IMPROVED: in the case of the real data you don't need a kernel, because you don't knoe the kernel. But without the kernel, the leaflet does not work. We have to fix this
Warning: [readValues] raster has no values
study_area_test$add_cases(dbase = outbreak_df)
study_area_test$add_inhabitants(real_data = TRUE)

Source tracing

Isotropic Kernel

This source tracing is done via Bayesian inference, using the Stan programming language. First we set up a simulation with one isotropic source.

study_area_test <- studyArea$new(res = 1000, municipality = "De Bilt",
                                 study_start_date = as_date("2023-01-01"),
                                 study_end_date = as_date("2023-02-01"))
study_area_test$add_inhabitants(200)
Warning: [readValues] raster has no values
study_area_test$add_kernel(k)
study_area_test$add_cases(dbase = NULL)
Warning: The `x` argument of `as_tibble.matrix()` must have unique column names if
`.name_repair` is omitted as of tibble 2.0.0.
ℹ Using compatibility `.name_repair`.
study_area_test$add_controls(ratio_controls_cases = 2)
plot(study_area_test)

Then, we run the Bayesian inference model

filename <- "test_model_fit.RDS"
model <- cmdstan_model(stan_file = here("stan_code", "sourcetracing_casebased.stan"),
                       dir = cmdstan_path())

if(!file.exists(here("data", "output", filename)) || params$recalc_stan){
  fit <- model$sample(
    data = study_area_test$as_stan_data(),
    seed = 123,
    iter_sampling = 1000,
    chains = 4,
    parallel_chains = 1,
    refresh = 0,
    show_messages = FALSE,
    show_exceptions = FALSE
  )
  fit$save_object(file = here("data", "output", filename))
} else {
  fit <- readRDS(here("data", "output", filename))
}

Reviewing the results

df_posterior <- fit %>%
  spread_draws(x_source[kernel], y_source[kernel],
               r0[kernel], h0[kernel], alpha[kernel])

df_posterior %>%
  pivot_longer(c(r0, h0, alpha), names_to = "param", values_to = "posterior") %>%
  left_join(study_area_test$get_kernel_params() %>%
              pivot_longer(c(r0, h0, alpha), names_to = "param", values_to = "true")) %>%
  ggplot() +
  stat_pointinterval(aes(x = posterior)) +
  geom_point(aes(x = true), y = 0, color = "red", size = 4) +
  facet_wrap(vars(param), scales = "free")
Joining with `by = join_by(kernel, param)`
df_posterior %>%
  ggplot() +
    geom_point(aes(x = x_source, y = y_source), alpha = 0.2, color = "#60B1F2") +
    geom_point(data = study_area_test$get_kernel_params(),
               aes(x = x, y = y, color = as.factor(kernel))) +
    coord_cartesian(xlim =  c(study_area_test$ext()[1], study_area_test$ext()[2]), ylim=c(study_area_test$ext()[3], study_area_test$ext()[4]))

Time Dependence

In the time dependent setting, the kernel is time dependent (due to daily varying wind, and the source “switching on” at some time), yielding a force of infection experienced by person \(i\) at location \(x_i\) and time \(t\) of \(\Psi(x_i, t)\). Also, cases have a day of onset \(t^*_i\). We redefine the probability of infection \(r(x_i)\) as the probability of becoming infected at time \(t*_i\), but not the days leading up to \(t^*_j\). The probability of infection at day \(t\) is \[ r(x_i, t) = 1-\exp(-\Psi(x_i,t)) \] which gives \[\begin{aligned} r(x_i) &= [1-\exp(-\Psi(x_i, t^*_i))]\prod_{t=1}^{t_i^*-1} \exp(-\Psi(x_i, t)\\ &= [1-\exp(-\Psi(x_i, t^*_i))]\exp(-\sum_{t=1}^{t^*_i-1} \Psi(x_i, t)) \end{aligned}\]

Define \(S_i(n) = \sum_{t=1}^n \Psi(x_i,t)\), then \[ r(x_i) =[1-\exp(-\Psi(x_i, t^*_i))]\exp(-S_i(t_i^*-1)) \] Controls were never infected, from day 1 up to the last day \(T\) of the study period. For them: \[ 1-r(x_i)=\exp(-\sum_{t=1}^{T} \Psi(x_i, j)) = \exp(-S_i(T)) \] Insert this in the likelihood

\[\begin{aligned} \log(L) &= \sum_{j=1}^J \log(r(x_j)) + \sum_{q=1}^Q \log(1-r(x_q)) \\ &= \sum_{j=1}^J \log((1-\exp(-\Psi(x_j, t^*_j))\exp(-S_j(t_j^*-1))) \\ &+ \sum_{q=1}^Q \log(\exp(-S_q(T))) \\ &= \sum_{j=1}^J \log(1-\exp(-\Psi(x_j, t^*_j))) -S_j(t_j^*-1) - \sum_{q=1}^Q S_q(T) \end{aligned}\]

Adding real data to the studyArea

Population

We have population data for the Netherlands that can be used for the calculation of n_inhabitants. There is a built-in option in the add_inhabitants option, to use the real CBS data.

study_area_test <- studyArea$new(
  res = 200,
  municipality = "De Bilt",
  the_crs = "epsg:28992",
  study_start_date = as_date("2021-01-25"),
  study_end_date = as_date("2021-02-01")
)

study_area_test$add_inhabitants(real_data = T)
Warning: [readValues] raster has no values
# Add women as well
study_area_test$add_inhabitants(real_data = T, lyrs = c("inwoner", "vrouw"))
# Use women as the value of n_inhabitants
study_area_test$add_inhabitants(real_data = T, lyrs = c("vrouw"))
study_area_test$plot()

Land-use (LGN)

Built in functions can be used for using major Land Use parameters. These can be considered as part of the study area or as descriptions of the surroundings of individuals, in which case they are considered covariates.

First we show how this property can be added to a study area and then to an individual.

study_area_test$add_lgn()
study_area_test$plot()

# Adding the LGN as covariates to an individual
individual_test <- individual$new(numberID = 1, x = 155000, y = 455000)
individual_test$add_covariates(radius = 20)
individual_test

# Adding the LGN data as covariates to individuals in a study area
k <- kernel$new(name = "test",
                x = 141470,
                y = 458960,
                r0 = 300,
                alpha = 3.0,
                h0 = 0.01)

study_area_test$add_kernel(k)
study_area_test$add_cases()
study_area_test$add_controls()
study_area_test$add_covariates(radius = 1000)

# Export force of infection for UTwente
study_area_test$export_foi("foi.nc")
study_area_test$get_cases()

Wind direction

The model can be anisotropic, meaning that the spread from the source is not the same in all directions. In reality this effect comes from the wind, blowing the particles away, making more particles end up down-wind from the source than upwind. The effect is implemented in the model based on the von Mises distribution, which is a normal distribution around a circle. In order to use the real wind direction data in our model we first need to convert it to the parameters of the von Mises distribution. These parameters are the location and the concentration . defines the mean angle and defines the spread. To obtain these values we fit the wind direction data of each day in the study period in the range of the study area, using stan. The and for each day are stored in a list within the studyArea object.

Case-control method on Legionella cases

# Load the Legionella outbreak data for Schijndel
outbreaks_filename <- here("data", "input", "TestDataLegionellaClusters_20231017_RDcoords.RDS")
outbreak_df <-  readRDS(outbreaks_filename) %>%
                filter(str_detect(RIVMLEGICLUSTER, "Schijndel"))

# Define the study dates based on outbreak data
study_dates <-  outbreak_df %>%
                mutate(DateOfOnset = as_date(DateOfOnset)) %>%
                select(DateOfOnset) %>%
                transmute(start = min(DateOfOnset), end = max(DateOfOnset)) %>%
                unique()

# Initialize the study area
study_area_test <- studyArea$new(
  res = 1000,  # Setting the spatial resolution
  study_start_date = study_dates$start,
  study_end_date = study_dates$end
)

# Add real inhabitants to the study area
study_area_test$add_inhabitants(real_data = TRUE)
Warning: [readValues] raster has no values
# Add cases and controls from the outbreak data
study_area_test$add_cases(dbase = outbreak_df)
study_area_test$add_controls(ratio_controls_cases = 2)

# Plot to visualize the study area, cases, and controls
study_area_test$plot()
# Define the kernel
k <- kernel$new(
  name = "test_kernel",
  x = 158500,   # Example x-coordinate
  y = 405000,   # Example y-coordinate
  r0 = 1000,    # Kernel radius
  alpha = 3.5,  # Kernel alpha
  h0 = 1.5      # Kernel height
)

# Add the kernel to the study area
study_area_test$add_kernel(k)

# Check the kernel parameters function
study_area_test$get_kernel_params()

# Prepare Stan model
stan_filepath <- here("stan_code", "sourcetracing_casebased.stan")
model <- cmdstan_model(stan_file = stan_filepath, dir = cmdstan_path())

# Define the Stan data using the study area
stan_data <- study_area_test$as_stan_data()

# Run the Stan model
output_file <- here("data", "output", "schijndel_fit.RDS")

if (!file.exists(output_file) || params$recalc_stan) {
  fit <- model$sample(
    data = stan_data,
    seed = 123,
    iter_sampling = 1000,
    chains = 4,
    parallel_chains = 4,
    refresh = 50  # Show occasional progress updates
  )
  fit$save_object(file = output_file)
} else {
  fit <- readRDS(output_file)
}

# Analyze posterior distributions
# Extract posterior draws
posterior_draws <- fit %>%
  spread_draws(x_source[kernel], y_source[kernel], r0[kernel], h0[kernel], alpha[kernel])

# Convert posterior draws into a long format
posterior_draws_long <- posterior_draws %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(r0, h0, alpha), 
    names_to = "param", 
    values_to = "posterior"
  )

# Obtain true kernel parameters from study area
kernel_params_long <- study_area_test$get_kernel_params() %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(r0, h0, alpha), 
    names_to = "param", 
    values_to = "true"
  )

# Join posterior draws with the true kernel parameters
merged_data <- posterior_draws_long %>%
  left_join(
    kernel_params_long, 
    by = "param"
  )

# Visualize posterior distributions and compare with true values
ggplot(merged_data, aes(x = posterior)) +
  stat_pointinterval() +  # Posterior intervals
  geom_point(aes(x = true, y = 0), color = "red", size = 4) +  # True parameter values
  facet_wrap(vars(param), scales = "free") +  # Plot for each parameter
  labs(title = "Posteriors vs true kernel parameters",
       x = "Posterior value",
       y = "Density",
       color = "Parameter") +
  theme_minimal()
